How Much Is a Used Ferrari 458 Spider Worth Today in USA?
12 photos
Photo: Instagram | motorcarsofchicago
Even though it’s been dead for many years, the Ferrari 458 continues to gain traction in our news feed, and if you wonder why, then you may want to throw away that petrolhead license, because you clearly do not need it.
Not only has this model aged like fine wine, but it is also the Prancing Horse’s last rear mid-engined, rear-wheel drive supercar to feature a naturally aspirated mill. Its successor, the 488, which was made between 2015 and 2020, is twin-turbocharged, and so is the F8 that followed from 2019 to 2023, whereas the modern-day 296 is not only turbocharged, but also partially electrified.
Ferrari made the 458 between 2009 and 2015 at its Maranello factory (where else?) in Italy. The F430’s successor is 178.2 inches (4,527 mm) long, 76.3 inches (1,937 mm) wide, and 47.8 inches (1,213 mm) tall. It has a wheelbase length of 104.3 inches (2,650 mm), a curb weight of a little over 1.5 metric tons (3,450 pounds), and was offered in two body styles: a two-door berlinetta (coupe) and a two-door convertible.
The lineup comprised the 458 Italia (Coupe), 458 Spider (Convertible), the 458 Speciale and Speciale A (Aperta / convertible), the 458 Italia China Edition, and the 458 MM Speciale, Pininfarina Sergio, and SP13 EC one-offs, which used the same underpinnings as the mainstream 458.
Photo: Instagram | motorcarsofchicago With this short history lesson behind us, it is time to put the spotlight on the Ferrari 458 Spider pictured above. It is a 2013 model year car, according to the vendor, and it features a glossy black look on the outside. It rides on black five-spoke alloys, has red brake calipers for a bit of contrast, and is decorated with the Prancing Horse logos all around.
Step inside, and you will see a mix of black leather and black Alcantara upholstery, wrapped around most touchable surfaces. There is also some carbon fiber trim, and we can see that this machine has red stitching for contrast, including on the seats, dashboard panel, door cards, and center console, black Prancing Horse emblems embroidered into the headrests, and a very simple and very cool overall layout compared to more modern supercars, this writer thinks.
There is only a tiny bit of wear on the driver’s seat outer bolster, so this particular Ferrari 458 Spider looks almost as good today as it did back when it originally left the dealership more than a decade ago. The vendor did not say much about it, so we do not know whether it has paint protection film on the outside, but the exterior also looks extremely fine, at least in the pictures that accompany the ad.
We do not know how many owners this machine has had over the years, no details surrounding the title have been released at the time of writing, and we also have no idea when it was last serviced. What we can tell you, though, is that the odometer read around 18,000 miles (29,000 km) at the time of cataloging.
Photo: Instagram | motorcarsofchicago Power is supplied by a 4.5-liter naturally aspirated V8 engine, which was good for 562 horsepower (570 ps/419 kW ) at 9,000 rpm and 398 pound-feet (540 Nm) of torque at 6,000 rpm back when the supercar was still new. The Ferrari 458 Italia , namely the fixed-roof model, took 3.4 seconds to hit 62 mph (100 kph) from a standstill, which made it some two-tenths of a second faster than the iconic Ferrari Enzo.
But what about the Ferrari 458 Spider, you ask? Well, with no outside intervention, it completed the sprint just as fast as the coupe, though its top speed was a tiny bit lower at 199 mph (320 kph), as opposed to the 458 Italia’s 202 mph (325 kph).
Depending on the mileage, options, and overall condition, a Ferrari 458 typically retails between $165,000 and over $450,000 in today’s used car market in the United States of America. The 458 Spider is a few tens of thousands more expensive than the 458 Italia, and models such as the 458 Speciale and 458 Speciale A can easily venture into the seven-digit realm.
Thus, your pockets must be quite deep if you dream about owning a 458, but does this also apply to the pictured example? In short, yes! That’s because this Italian supercar is on the very pricey side of things. We found it advertised on social media by @motorcarsofchicago, with an asking price of $379,995 attached to it at the time of writing.
The vendor says it accepts trade-ins, offers financing, and is not particularly fond of DMs. Therefore, you know what to do if you want to sign your name on the dotted line of this 2013 Ferrari 458 Spider , don’t you? But is this supercar worth the asking price, or do you feel like it is a bit too much? View this post on Instagram A post shared by Motor Cars of Chicago (@motorcarsofchicago)
